newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Power-starved Bangladesh seeks foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Power-starved Bangladesh seeks foreign investment.

text.p: Power-starved Bangladesh is considering importing electricity from abroad and has drawn up a plan to attract private investment in the power sector, government officials say.
A shortfall of up to 350 megawatts during peak hours was threatening industrial production and economic growth, a top energy ministry official told Reuters on Wednesday.
The problem turned from bad to worse with the recent shutdown of two 270-megawatt power plants in the south after production in the Bakhrabad gas field fell sharply, he said.

"The power crisis is serious," he said. "We have only two options at the moment -- one is importing electricity from neighbouring countries and the other is setting up barge-mounted power plants by the private sector."

He said the government was studying the possibility of importing power from India. Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in September said Bangladesh was considering buying electricity from abroad but she did not say which countries.
The opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party and several fringe parties have said they would resist any attempt to procure electricity from India.
"We will (also) have two barge-mounted power plants on a build-own-operate (BOO) basis by the private sector," the ministry official said.

Energy ministry officials said the two plants with a total capacity of producing 220 MW could be set up within a year. The government was trying to firm up deals with private sector companies, the official said but gave no details.
Officials said five of 11 foreign companies which had signed memoranda of understading (MOU) would also bid for setting up another 100-200 MW capacicty plant on BOO basis.
The ministry official said a 300 MW plant would be built within three years. The Asian Development Bank and a foreign firm would set up the plant with equity participation.
Five major companies, including Asea Brown Boveri AG of Germany, Marubeni Corp of Japan and GETCO of Malaysia, had been short-listed for investment in the 300 MW plant.
The official also said U.S. companies showed "tremendous interest" in power sector investment during Hasina's visit to the United States last month.

The government had formulated a new private sector power generation policy to attract foreign and local investment. "We expect all power generation to be done by the private sector from now on," he said.
The present power generation companies are in the public sector. But he ruled out any possibility of privatisation.
Bangladesh says it needs to achieve economic growth at a rate of six to seven percent to alleviate poverty. Gross domestic product growth is currently running at 4.7 percent.

"To achieve the growth target of GDP, it is absolutely essential that the minimum electricity growth rate is maintained at a factor of 1.5 of GDP growth," the new policy statement published last month said.
It said only 15 percent of Bangladesh's 120 million population currently had access to electricity. The per capita generation is only 95 kilowatt hours a year.
The policy suggests $6.6 billion investment in power generation from 1996 to 2005. It said peak demand would rise from the present 2,200 MW to 3,150 by 2000 and 4,600 by 2005.

"The likelihood of securing such a substantial volume of investment for power generation alone through the public sector is remote," the policy said. "(So) the government is strongly committed to attract private investment."
